utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. If I might have a new introduction here, if you will give me a moment, I would love to introduce to the court Judge John Ackerman from the United States, who is a new member of the defence team. Also on behalf of everyone on the defence team I would like to express how happy we are to see Judge Jan back and healthy again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This is Judge Ackerman from the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning. I am very pleased and honoured to be here. It is nice to see you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you. We welcome you here to enjoy the company of an excellent team. Can we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg. I appear today, as before, with my learned friends Mr. Giuliano Turone, Ms. Teresa McHenry and Ms. Elles van Dusschoten. I also want to express my happiness and welcome back in his seat His Honour Judge Jan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we have appearances on the side of the defence, please? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honour. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me is Professor Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I am Michael Greaves. I act on behalf of the Defendant Zdravko Mucic. I am fortunate today to be assisted by Ms. Mira Taposovic. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, Mr. Karabdic. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, defence counsel of Mr. Hazim Delic. With me is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning again, your Honours. My name is Cynthia McMurrey. I am here on behalf of Esad Landzo with Judge John Ackerman from the United States and Mr. Mustafa Brackovic, who is just not present in the court room at this time, all three representing Mr. Landzo at this point. I wanted to ask the court's tolerance. I have a matter that will require my absence from the court room tomorrow for the rest of the week, and I am just seeking approval from the court that I not be present, but everything will be taken care of and we will feel very comfortable. Mr. Landzo has approved my absence from the court room at this time. I just wanted to inform the court. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Ms. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now we have before us a motion which I just was very curious about, because I do not know whether there can be a ruling on it about the question of cross-examination and the like. I do not know what actually it is all about. Counsel have submitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will inform your Honour. Thank you. Since we filed our motion seeking a decision on the scope of cross-examination, the Chamber has on 1st May ruled on a motion on presentation of evidence by the accused, Esad Landzo. We totally agree with all what we can read in that decision. In paragraph 22 of that decision the Trial Chamber says, among other things: "The object of cross-examination is two-fold: first, to elicit information concerning facts in issue or relevant to issue, that is favourable to the party on whose behalf the cross-examination is conducted." Then it goes on on that question. The Prosecution takes it that the Trial Chamber thereby has ruled that cross-examination is indeed permitted on any relevant issue and that re-examination would be allowed on any relevant issue, and that re-examination would be allowed also on the issue arising from the cross-examination. We, therefore, your Honours, withdraw our motion. However, we stay with the views presented in our brief, and it was mainly a brief, and a very short part of it was a motion, and we hope that it still can be of some assistance to the Chamber. I will not take up your time proceeding to reiterate what we have stated in that brief. Thank you, your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Actually personally I regarded it as a very good position paper, not necessarily any matter in contention, because I did not see anything from which a Ruling should be made on the issues which were raised there, because this Tribunal I would say is not intended for determining hypothetical issues. We determine actual issues. If there should be a contention between counsel arising from a motion, we should give it every attention. I did not think it was necessary, but since it was raised and very good papers were written, even on the part of the defence, we thought we should give it some hearing. Have you anything about it on the part of the defence? Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Tom Moran for Hazim Delic. I just wanted to say we agree with the court that these matters are things that have to be ruled on as they arise. There is no reason to write a treatise on the law of evidence. Rule 89(b) gives the Trial Chamber the discretion to make these kinds of Rulings as they arise. Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have nothing to add to the response that was filed on behalf of Mr. Mucic on 22nd April. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Any other views on it? I suppose, the motion having been withdrawn, I think the less said about it ... So we can now proceed with the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it was cross-examination of Mr. Golubovic, and he is here. Thank you. (Witness entered court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Kindly remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (in interpretation): I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it is cross-examination. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. Ms. McMurrey, it is you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honours. I cannot see the witness because this camera is right in the way. Could I ask somebody to move that, please? (Pause.) Thank you very much. May I proceed, your Honour? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. MIRO GOLUBOVIC Cross-examined by MS. McMURREY

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Golubovic. Welcome back. You were such a wonderful witness before we had this break in responding to the questions that if you do not understand any question I ask, please feel free to say: "I don't understand." Also if I ask a question, I am asking you to please listen to it and just answer the question I am asking, please. Can we have an agreement on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was ten days ago we were here, I think. It is difficult picking up. I am going to try not to repeat anything. My first question is: before you ever came to testify, when you were still back at your home, the Prosecution notified you to make a decision on whether you wanted to discuss your testimony with the defence, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told them that you did not want to talk to us ahead of time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told them that I do want to talk, but I do not know what purpose that would have, but I wanted to talk in the presence of the Public Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did tell them that you would visit with us in their presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would have loved to have had that opportunity. You spoke to the prosecution, I believe it was in November 1996, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not with the prosecution; with a gentleman who is not here present in this hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was not a member of the prosecution team present, just the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke to this gentleman. I do not know who he was, whether -- I don't know what his official post is. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we had this long break in the trial, did you travel back to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you discussed your testimony or the events that happened in Celebici with anybody while you were present at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't see many people. I just met with my family and I told them how I came here, but nothing specific about the trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is your occupation still a car mechanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a driver and a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And driver, you are a taxi driver; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not driving a taxi, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 you were a taxi driver in Konjic, though, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a taxi driver in the Konjic area, you got to know everybody in the area, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992 Cerici was predominantly a Serbian village, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only in 1992. As far back as I can remember it was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you could have voted or you may have voted in the referendum that was offered to you all on March 1st, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not vote. I didn't vote at the other referendum for the parties even. I didn't vote even then. I don't know whether I ever actually voted in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you are not a very politically active person. Is that not what you told us before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: if you had wanted to vote in the referendum, you would have been qualified to vote in the referendum, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I had the right to vote. Nobody was preventing me from doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were first arrested on May 6th, 1992 or some place like that, when you were driving your taxi near the Motel Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then they took you to the Motel Konjic and asked you a lot of questions and searched your apartment. I guess they were looking for weapons; is that the assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were detained in the motel for how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the motel; in the public security station, five or six hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The public security station, is that close to the Motel Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe some 3 kms. away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of the war, in May of 1992, you lived on 15th September Street in Konjic at apartment number 19, did you not? I guess I got the apartment right. I do not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apartment 24-9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You lived -- this apartment complex that you lived in was next to the apartment complex that Esad Landzo lived in, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you knew Esad Landzo before the war, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, but I knew his younger brother better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His younger brother, Suad, or Sudo I think is his name, he helped you wash cars and paint a trailer on several occasions, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you were so popular that all of the neighbourhood kids wanted to spend a lot of time with you, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can call that popularity, but I liked mixing with children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the village of Cerici was attacked on May 19th, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 19th or 20th. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time your father had been negotiating with the HVO for a peaceful surrender of the village; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father and some other neighbours called up people by phone. I don't know whether it was the HVO, but they called up Konjic, asking them to stop shelling and to agree on the surrendering of arms, and for them to come to Celebici to make statements, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father, his name is -- pardon my massacring the language -- I think it is Slavajub Golubovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He peacefully surrendered, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He went to the village, brought his hunting rifle. He was allowed to go home. Then he was called up again and they took him to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what day your father was taken to Celebici, or did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was one or two days after the village fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So maybe around May 21st; would that be close? 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it didn't go with the first group, but I can't say exactly what date it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time that the village fell, you were armed, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was. That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry. I forgot what kind of weapon you said you had. Could you just tell me again, because I forgot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a machine gun, 762 mms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a World War II issue machine gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is a more recent production.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am ignorant about weapons pretty much. At the time that the village fell you became a fugitive at that point, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had the TO, the HVO and MUP looking for you all at the same time, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't notice anyone looking for me, but probably they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did say that you became a member of the SDS in March of 1992, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around there, maybe a couple of months before the war broke out, but there are documents to confirm this. There is no problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just because we were not there, would you just explain to the Trial Chamber what the SDS was to you in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me in March 1992 the SDS was the same for me as HDZ was for Catholics and SDA for Muslims.. I can give you a popular saying that we have in our land, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would say: "Where all the Turks go, little Mojo goes as well", which means one goes with the flock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the ethnic separation then of the Serbians, Muslims and Croats basically; is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but my participation in the party, you can imagine how important it was when I joined only a couple of months. You can imagine how important I was for them and what kind of function I had. None really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except I believe you stated that your mother shamed you into participating in the patrols of your village; is that right -- not shamed you, but said that you should do that; it was your duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That may seem funny or strange, but that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not funny. You were funny the other day the way you explained it and I remember that. You also said that your mother --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my mother who told me to come here to testify. If it weren't for her, I would never have come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Moran's mother told him to come here too, so that is why he is here. You say that your mother negotiated your surrender to the MUP. Was that your testimony a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She negotiated with the military police of the Croatian defence council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you surrendered or you were captured? Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I surrendered to the HVO in front of my house in the village of Cerici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You surrendered with Milovan Kuljanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also known as Mici; is that his nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your mother was communicating with -- was it Darko Verkic? Is that his name, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, madam, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What your belief was and what your mother's belief was was that she had negotiated with Mr. Verkic to have you sent on to the safe territory in Croatia? Is that what she was working on, what her intention in the negotiation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Her aim was to have me surrender to the Croatian Defence Council to be taken to Celebici together with my neighbours to make a statement, as I had no reason to be afraid of anything, so I was not afraid to go to Celebici. The only problem was that I had stayed behind the others some ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said it was ten days today that you were a fugitive, but you have said before that it was fifteen days, and if Milovan Kuljanin said it was 20 days, would he be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, the village fell on 22nd or 21st. I reached the camp on 6th and all that time I was a fugitive and Milovan Kuljanin with me too, so there is no problem there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Milovan Kuljanin said you all surrendered on 10th, 11th or 12th, would he be incorrect then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would not be correct. I have on my watch inscribed the date when I surrendered, on 6th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So if Milovan Kuljanin stated that his understanding was that you all were going to make a statement to the Croatians and then be taken on to a safe area outside of Bosnia, that would not be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how he understood it, but I know what I thought, what I expected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived at Celebici, were you interviewed immediately when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I spent a couple of hours in the manhole and then I was taken to make a statement to Mladen Zovko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That manhole you describe now, is that the one at the far end of the camp here, I believe? If you want to stand up, I think it is the one you testified about; is that at the very end of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I would like the record to reflect that he has pointed at the manhole at the very far end of Celebici, as far away from the gate as you can get, I believe. Inside that manhole was dry and there was no water or anything in there, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could feel -- you could smell the urine. There was a platform, a metal platform, so I wasn't paying much attention whether there was water or not, but that day I was not in the water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you supply that watch that you inscribed with the date that you arrived at Celebici to the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody asked that watch of me. I didn't bring it with me either and nobody asked it of me. I wasn't asked to give up either a watch or money in Celebici. They even left my shoelaces and belt that I wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you still have that watch in your possession; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my watch I do have on me, in my possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that some time in the future, when Mr. Golubovic is allowed to return to his home that we be at least provided with some kind of documentation showing that he -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What is the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It goes to alibi. He says he saw Mr. Landzo the day he came to the camp. He says it is June 6th. We say it is another date. It is very important, the inscription on the watch. If it says June 6th, I would ask the court to provide us with that documentation some time in the future. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The inscription he made on his watch?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. May we ask the court to have that provided to us at a future date? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We are not supposed to do that. I think you ask the prosecution to know what to do about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know anything about a watch or where it is, so I do not ... I do not believe that anything more is necessary beyond this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, we believe that it is necessary for the defence of alibi that we have raised a long time ago, and the alibi is that Mr. Landzo was present in the camp in the middle of June. If he claims he saw him on the day that he was brought in, this is very relevant to our defence. I think we have a right to have that provided for us. We had no idea that there was documentation until this witness testified. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is your own defence, is it not? It is your own defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, it is Mr. Landzo's defence. I am just asking -- we would hate to have to call this witness back again. If that can be provided, we move right along, and no other problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It was not clear to me from the witness's answer. Maybe he can be asked if he has the watch here in the Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He said he had it back at his home. He doesn't have it with him. I don't know if I have a ruling on that, but I would like to have that -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not see what the business of that ruling is, whether he is to provide you with your alibi. That is what you are trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just trying to get the documentation that he just testified about. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He has told you he inscribed it in his watch and you want the watch in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would either like the watch in, or just a photograph of the watch showing the inscription would be sufficient for us, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If he is able to provide it, he is still here. Ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, could you provide me with a photograph of the watch with your inscription of "June 6th, 1992" on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the date 6th June, when I arrived there, but I can give you the watch. It doesn't work any more. Mr. Landzo was at the door of the camp that evening, and he had an M-48 rifle with the "TO" inscribed on it. I know that very well, because Delic wanted to interrogate me and Landzo wanted to hit me. He said: "No, no, no, he's my bird. Leave him alone." So I know that he was there, because when they were burning me, he was learning it at that time. So please don't do that now, because this is certain, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I am asking is: would you be willing to return here to The Hague with the watch, if we asked you to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why not, but I can write it or something. What is much more important, the documents that I can provide, my release form, when I was taken in and when I was released. I think that's much more important, but if you want the watch, I can bring the watch. I wasn't lying about that watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not accusing you of lying and I appreciate your strategy for what you think is important in this case, but I am counsel for Mr. Esad Landzo and I am trying to determine what is important to build the case over here also. Please be tolerant with me and understand that I am just doing my job right now. I am sure that we will be able to work out some documentation to provide for that in the future. I feel free that you and I will communicate on that or I will communicate through the prosecution. Thank you. When you were brought in that day, you said you were interrogated by Darko Verkic; is that correct, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was questioned by Mladen Zovko. I gave my first statement to Mladen Zovko and there was also another gentleman there who I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zovko also known as Kuhar; is that correct? Is that his nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a friend of yours before the war, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We grew up together. We grew up in the same street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He did not beat you. There were no problems.. You were treated correctly at the time you were interviewed by Mr. Kuhar, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. He took down my statement correctly but as far as his behaviour is concerned, he was correct with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though he was a close friend of yours, he placed you into one of the three categories at Celebici, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somebody did. I don't know if it was him or someone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the category you were placed in was the most dangerous category, I think, because you had a weapon and you were taken to Tunnel Number 9, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I just object? Can I just clarify exactly what the question is? It seemed to me there were several questions in there. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That when you arrived at the camp, you were categorised in one of the most dangerous categories, the category 3, because you had a weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what category I was. I know that after the questioning I was taken to Number 22 and then later they mistreated me, and after that they took me to Number 9, and for the groups I only heard about those. You said number 3. I have also heard that I was category number 1 as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just for clarification, you know the HVO left Celebici you had stated about ten days after you arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about ten days. After about ten days I stopped seeing their soldiers there except for one young man, who remained there, who became a member of the TO, and the rest I did not see there after that. They would come every once in a while, but I did not see them working there or being on duty there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be correct that the HVO left Celebici some time around June 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to go back a few minutes, so if Mici said that you all surrendered after 20 days, and if he said that you were brought to Celebici on June 11th, then that would not be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought to Celebici on 6th June together with Mici. Maybe they took him somewhere and then brought him back. I don't know how he can say that he got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Konjic during this time there was no free travel for everybody within the municipality, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some could and some could not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were close friends with a Mr. Zivak, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Spaso Zivak? You mean Spaso Zivak?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I have is a last name, so I don't know. Did you have many friends named Zivak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was friends with all people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have realised that. Thank you. That is true. The weapons that were distributed in Cerici, they were distributed by former JNA and SDA members, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know who I got my weapons from, but -- and I can't even say how much I can claim it as my own. It was simply in my possession at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had received your weapon from Strajo Zivak, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I received it from Dragan Sinikovic. If you thought about my friendship with Strajo Zivak, I have to say that we didn't even know each other. In retrospect I wish that maybe we did know each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that period were you familiar with the political situation in Donje Selo at the time, since Cerici is very close to Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Konjic, and I would infrequently go to Cerici, and the political situation, if there was any there, I don't know what you have in mind. Can you ask me a different question, something specific?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I will ask you something specific. Were you aware that the village of Donje Selo held out and had resistance with the promise from the Serbian forces that they would come in and assist them in this resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about the defence. We didn't have any trenches or anything. There were some armed individuals there, maybe about 30 people with the weapons, and they were turned in at Celebici and that was all the defence, all the organisation. We had no people who would be able to command. One day it was one person; another day it was another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you surrendered, you turned in your weapon and all the ammunition along with it, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe once you mentioned a group called the Lozice group? Can you tell me what that was? You said you did not see them when you were a fugitive. L-O-Z-I-C-E?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't understand. There was something missing in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You once stated that you did not see this Lozice group when you were a fugitive. What was this group that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I did not see any group that was looking for me, the HVO, MUP or any other. That's what I said and I am not familiar with the name of the group that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you were interviewed at Celebici the type of questions that were asked were regarding the arming of the Serbian population and about your weapons, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not. They once asked me whether I drove any weapons for the SDS, but that is not true. I didn't even have an opportunity for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us on your direct examination how you were tortured and beaten when you first came to Celebici. Are you aware that the sole purpose of that beating was to locate weapons? Was that the kind of questions they were asking you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Again, if I may just object to the compound question, it is not clear to me what the question is, so the record is clear. May I just ask that there be one question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I can repeat it, but I think it was one question with the preface he told us before about the time that he was seriously beaten by Bato Alkadic I believe was his name. While he was being beaten, did they make it clear to him that they were looking for arms and weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bato Alkadic was asking me some questions from our private lives, while we lived well together, when we were friends, but he also did ask me where my father's hunting weapons were, that is correct, and he also asked me whether I knew him, whether I was lending him money, whether I was towing his car from Istanbul, those kinds of questions I was asked by Mr. Alkadic. I told him all that and he said: "Okay. That's all right. Never mind that. We are not friends any more and we are not friends and Zjelko Klimenta is not a friend any more." He said, "Kneel down." I knelt and he started to perform his ritual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is so hard for us to try to understand how one minute you have close friends and the next minute you do not. That must have been very difficult on you too at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had I known that Bato Alkadic was in the Celebici camp, I would not have been a fugitive for ten minutes, let alone ten days. I would have come straight to him. I wouldn't have thought about the Celebici camp. I would have preferred to -- I would have preferred to surrender to Bato Alkadic than to my own father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you also told us the other day about how you were burned in the administration building during an interview. The person who tortured you that day --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- his name was Narcis, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if that is his first or last name or his nickname, but I know that he was a warrant-officer in the former JNA. He was the Commander of that Celebici compound before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that they were questioning you, they made it clear to you that two policemen had been killed by a sniper and that you were one of the suspects in that case. Did they not say that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were not mentioning that at that time. Had they done that that night, I don't think I would have been able to sit here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was mentioned to you at some time in May, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a justification later on, so that they would justify themselves in front of some friends of theirs, who were asking them why they did this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated there was no clear organised structure at Celebici when you arrived. That is true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, as far as I could infer and see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, after the HVO pulled out, there was more chaos in the camp, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the time when I was in the camp, which was in the beginning, it was the same every day. After the Red Cross visit I wasn't there and the inmates say that the situation did improve later, but between 6th June and 17th July it was the same. You couldn't see any improvements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that there was no clear indication of who was commander of the camp during this chaotic period; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. I did not see the insignia and I didn't understand them. The policemen had the insignia, but not the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the policemen, this was the military police, who were free to come and go at Celebici as they chose; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the civilian police, and I think that it just grew into the military police. I don't know. Before the war they were for the most part members of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was clear that there were guards and there were other people who commanded the guards, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody was ordering me when I was in Number 9. I was not able to see the commanding ... People who were in Number 6 were getting out much more and could see who was ordering whom and what. I had no opportunity to see anybody ordering someone to do this or that. To us it was the guards who were coming to us and they were taking people out if they needed to be questioned; or if they needed to beat him, they would take him out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were what might be called the casual detainee in Celebici, and I mean by that that you had a lot more freedom as a detainee there than any of the other prisoners, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how you mean "casual". I could go out when I was in the hospital. I could go to the toilet and to drink water and sometimes I would be taken out to pick up cigarette butts and papers, to clean. I don't know if you see that as freedom of movement. That was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also were given easier jobs in the camp like cleaning the weapons. That was one of the jobs, the duties you performed sometimes, and working on automobiles. Did you not do both of those at Celebici too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. On one occasion I did clean the rifles that were found in the field and a few times I did repair cars; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you were allowed to sit outside with the guards and you visited with them on a friendly basis most of the time you were there, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I was not talking -- there was no guard in front of the administration building and Number 22. There was no guard there. That was close to the administration building, so there was no need for them to be there, so I did not talk to them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were able to walk around in that area and be outside in the sunlight. In fact, you had so much freedom that Mr. Mucic had asked you not to go near the fence, because you might get mistaken for someone trying to escape, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, but they would tell me to go and clean near the fence. I never went out -- I never left Number 22 in order to take a walk, only if I was asked to go and do something. It would have been very dangerous for me to go out and take a walk around. Perhaps somebody found that it was good for me, but my opinion is that it was not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did get to visit with Mr. Landzo, just visiting with him outside of Number 22, did you not, during this time, just cordial greetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I -- did I understand you correctly, that you said I went to visit Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, when he was off duty standing around 22 or the guard house, that you would all visit and exchange pleasantries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I did talk to Landzo. I remember that, and it had to do with some hunt and some meadow that could be seen from the camp, but Mr. Landzo did not mistreat me in the camp, and I think that that is sufficient. I cannot say that he mistreated me when he did not. I cannot talk to our cordiality very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, when you talked about Mr. Narcis, he was putting the hot whatever it was on you in the administration building, Mr. Landzo was not present then, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was on guard duty in front of the building. He was not present in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was night-time, when that occurred, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was night-time; correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So because you were not outside of Tunnel 9 very often, but you did get to see the activities from 22 going on, was it clear -- it was clear that guards were following orders most of the time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably somebody ordered them some things. Some things maybe they did on their own, the way they wanted. I did not hear them being ordered, like: "Take Golubovic out and beat him by the fence." Had I heard that, I would have stated that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony is you did not hear the order, but it could have been ordered; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably some things were ordered to them. They can be ascertained. This can be found out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I do not remember whether you discussed the food at Celebici before, but you knew that the food came in a van from the outside of Celebici, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was brought there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, that same van brought the same food for the guards and for the detainees, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it was the same I don't know, but when this van arrived -- actually it was a Lada caravan -- Ustalic was driving it. I can't remember exactly who it was later. Whether it was the same food or not I don't know. I think it wasn't. We were given bread mostly; occasionally some rice and some beans, three spoonfuls each.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have Prosecution Exhibit number 1 offered to Mr. Golubovic at this time for his review, to refer to some of the photographs, if the usher would please give it to him. (Handed). Mr. Golubovic, these are the photographs that the prosecution has put into evidence referring to the camp at Celebici. I am going to ask you, number one, if you will just take a moment and thumb through and look at all of the photographs just for a moment and see if that looks familiar to you. In a moment, so that the computer people can be apprised, I am going to ask that we publish on to the monitor Prosecution Photographs, number 23, 24, 25 and 26, please. Mr. Golubovic -- can I get those photographs, if possible, or is this too short notice?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe, although I cannot speak for them about the notice, I believe you could certainly put them on the ELMO from the original exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That would be just fine, if Mr. Usher would like to put 23 on the -- I think we have a difference here in numbering. I am not sure. If the usher would check and see if number 23 is a photograph of Building Number 22.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we have it on there? Thank you. Mr. Golubovic, if you could -- you could identify this as Building Number 22 or the infirmary in June of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were held in this building longer than you were any place else while you were in Celebici; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, roughly about the same time as in Number 9. More actually. Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then could I also have 24, 25 and 26 just displayed? This is the backside of Building Number 22, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 25 and 26, if we might publish those for a second, those show what is now the inside of Number 22, but it didn't look like that in 1992, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, those shelves were not there and these pump things were not there in 1992, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I reached 22, they were not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These four photographs, these are the total photographs that the prosecution has introduced with regard to Building Number 22, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to that. How would this witness know exactly what the prosecution has and has not put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will clarify that. In this document that you have looked at, these are the only photographs of Number 22 that they have in Prosecution Exhibit number 1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to look through the book again. There may be another photograph. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to look through the book again but I want you to refer to the photograph that is in front of you. The window in number 26 where the pumps -- the next photograph -- that window goes out to the back of Building Number 22, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 those windows on either end were the same milk glass that is in the middle of these windows, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that. I know I was looking through this window while it was one quarter open, as much as it could be. That was the system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are looking at photograph number 26, and the window is open. That is as far as this window would open, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only that far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are telling the court right now you cannot remember whether that was clear or milk glass in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I see on the photograph that you can see through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if the other witnesses said in 1992 that this was milk glass, you would not know whether that was incorrect or not, would you, because you cannot remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am saying again that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this window is maybe 1.9 metres up, is it not? It is taller than I am in the building, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It is quite high up, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could not look through that window without standing on something to peer out; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would stand on the bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now to look back through all of the photographs, if you would just quickly. I am asking you: does the prosecution have a photograph in there showing what the view is from that window towards Tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could see through that window the entrance to Tunnel Number 9, perhaps some 20 metres to the left, and maybe even more towards the left, and to the right maybe some 20 metres this tap could be seen, the water tap that we used to drink from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was that there is no photograph reflecting the view from that window towards Tunnel Number 9, is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could we just have the witness, if he can, tell us the number of the photograph he is referring to when he says: "You could see this tap"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 45. It's number 45. You could see more than can be seen on the photograph. The field of vision was greater than you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry. What photograph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 45, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is just the front of Tunnel 9, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the entrance to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: there is no photograph from the window of 22 to Tunnel 9, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who took these photographs and where from they were taken. It is rather a complicated question for me. If you can give me a big photograph or you can take me to Celebici, I can show you how much I could see. How do I know which photograph was taken and what kind of technique was used?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not know how many photographs were taken, but in this exhibit there is no photograph that is taken from the point of view -- from the window in Building 22 to Tunnel 9, is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered. The witness has said he does not know the answer. I think the Chamber has already had evidence from the person who took the photographs about this. The witness has already answered that he does not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has not given me an answer to the question that I asked. I am just asking: is there one that reflects that point of view in the prosecution's exhibit? May I continue? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. Ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no photograph from the point of view of the window of Building 22 to Number 9, is there, in this exhibit? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, if you have seen one, kindly mention it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: There is none. That is why I want the court to realise that -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Then why do you ask him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Because I want him to say "no" from where -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Why do you know there is one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Because I have looked at it twice. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Then if you can ask any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. So my question is: there are no other photographs from that point of view, are there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is this photograph number 23, 26. That could have been taken from the window in the direction of Number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was not, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was taken from within Building 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to ask you to also look at the front of the prosecution's exhibit there, and I do not know what it is called. There is a scale drawing of the camp like this. (Indicating). It says "Number 1" at the top, but I am not sure what exhibit this is. Could you open that for us, please? Does this look like a scale of Celebici to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just testified, just a few moments ago, that you thought it was about 20 metres from 22 to Tunnel 9; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. I testified that from the window I could see from the entrance to Number 9, 20 metres to one side and 20 metres to the other. We would always see the entrance, the detainees when they went to drink water, to bathe, when they went to the toilet. There was a pit here. You probably know where this field toilet was. That's what I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this scale drawing we have here reflects the distance from the window at Building Number 22 to Tunnel 9 is really from about 70-80 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand how you manage to calculate it, but it was something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just using --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly 50. 50. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are certain things on these drawings and these models that were not reflected on this model, like the gigantic concrete banks at the end of the railway station. There were two big banks at the end of the railway station that are about 3 metres high, are there not -- not 3 metres, 2 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were banks at the end of the rails, and there were banks of sand on them, and the guards were practising shooting there. I never saw any kind of embankment made of concrete or anything else. These were simple barriers, concrete barriers in case a truck should pass, and it would stop there, and on top of them were sacks with sand, which were used as shooting targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were released from Celebici on July 17th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that the day that you were to be released Mr. Esad Landzo brought in a Mr. Bosko Samoukovic into the infirmary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he brought him into the infirmary, that was July 17th then, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was given my discharge papers on 17th July. That is what it said on the paper. Whether it was 17th, 16th, 15th or 18th I cannot recollect exactly, but the day I left the camp Mr. Landzo brought Mr. Samoukovic to Number 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could have gotten your release papers on the 17th, but you could have left Celebici earlier than that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably I could have left later, not earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Landzo brought Mr. Samoukovic to Number 22, he seemed very frightened, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who is who, just so the record is clear, Mr. Samoukovic or --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Mr. Landzo appeared to be very frightened, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was lying on the bed and I didn't see them when he brought him in. I know that he said that they should treat him and bring him to Number 6 in half an hour. I think there was other detainees with him, but I don't know exactly who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is you didn't see when he brought Mr. Samoukovic to Number 22, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard his voice. I didn't see him that very moment, but I saw him later, when he came in, and asked me why I was afraid to lie on the bed on which Samoukovic had died. I was sitting on the bed. I wasn't lying on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July of 1992 Mr. Landzo was very young, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how old Mr. Landzo is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you knew he had just gotten out of high school, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. It is no secret how old Mr. Landzo is. It is easy to find out how old he is now and how old he was then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how old did you know that he was in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly how old he was. I don't even know now how old he is. I am not quite sure myself how old I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew in the camp there was a woman named Ismeta Posder, was there not? Did you know Miss Posder as the secretary at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Miss Ismeta Posder. I would see her in the canteen. She gave me some sugar, but I didn't know what her function was in the camp. She'd give me cigarettes, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew another detainee named Zarko Mrkajic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Zarko Mrkajic. I still know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was also a casual detainee, was he not? I mean, he was allowed freedom as you were, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zarko Mrkajic would come from Number 9. I would take food and take it to Number 9. I would come to take water. I would see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he would even come into the administration building and drink with the guards, would he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see him doing that. It is possible. If somebody said so or if somebody saw him, then probably it is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what "Zenga" means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of the bar of people's guards of the Croatian army, the people's guards of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo's nickname was "Zenga", was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was more like the Croatians? Is that what the name meant, or does it have any other meaning to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't give him that name, so I really don't know. Maybe they wanted to be Zengas in those days and not now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I have one moment, your Honours, to review? (Pause.) On the exhibit, the model here for Celebici, can you point on the model to the room where Mr. Narcis interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That front room there. That was at night-time; is that correct -- I am sorry. Now Mr. Narcis was not a member of the guards at Celebici, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, he was really just a visitor at the camp that day. What military group did he belong to? The military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came with members of the Ministry of the Interior. Which formations he belonged to I don't know. They addressed him as "Captain, sir".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware too that right towards the end of your stay at Celebici there was an incident where nine military police were killed, murdered out at Repovci? Is that the name of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it while I was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Landzo had a very close friend that was murdered up there at that time, his neighbour on 15th September Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about the high concrete embankments at the end of the railroad tracks a while ago, and you described some sand bags that were on there. How high did the sand bags go from the top of the concrete embankments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not on top of the concrete slabs, but they were piled up against the concrete slabs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not testify that something occurred on the top of the concrete slabs? I do not remember what it was. Did they unload things from the top or what was it that you said about the top?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would put bottles and shoot them as practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I am going to ask you your tolerance. It is break time, and I am about to wrap this up, but I have one photograph that we have in the defence room that I would like to question him on when we return. If we might just break two minutes early, I will be completely finished within five minutes when we return, if I can just be allowed to get that photograph. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We will break for 30 minutes. I think that should give you ample opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you for your tolerance. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Trial Chamber will rise and reassemble at 12. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00 noon) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the witness and continue where we stopped? (Witness returned to court)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while we bring the witness in, I just want to clarify for the record, not necessarily with the witness, that defence counsel were given a letter about the possibility that this witness might be willing to give a pre-trial interview. It is not something the witness knows about, the letter, but I just wanted to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. McHenry and I did discuss that. I never received the letter but I do not doubt it may have been lost somewhere in our shuffle over here. I appreciate the fact that she made us aware of that. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. You can now continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If the usher might one more time provide Mr. Golubovic with the Prosecution Exhibit number 1, I would appreciate it. I would like to tell the court once I reviewed our photographs back here they do not show what we needed to show, so we are going to leave them alone right now. Thank you. Number 8. That should be a photograph, I believe, of the front of the command centre. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Golubovic, does that represent to you the front of the command centre, which is the area facing Building Number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to go back on one area, the night that Mr. Narcis did those things to you during his interview, would you point on the photograph which room you were located in? Over on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing). Here to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The location where you see this guard standing or this soldier standing, is that the location that you say you saw Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Landzo here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I would like to have this document marked as Defence Exhibit, if the usher can do so many things at one time. Ask Mr. Roeland to mark that as Defence Exhibit. Could I have it handed to Mr. Golubovic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It is his statement from Celebici camp, your Honour, with his signature on it. I was going to ask him to clarify that for you. I also have our interpretations of it in English, which, after it is -- I would like to offer these to the court. The prosecution has been provided with a copy of this already. Thank you. I did not hear what number that is marked. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let him see them first. We have not heard his opinion about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Golubovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this document was not presented to you and that is not your signature on the back page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, your Honours, then I will move on. Just a couple more questions. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So what is the proposal?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I cannot introduce it into evidence, if he does not recognise it, your Honour, so I will withdraw these at this moment. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your impression of Mr. Landzo was that he was a young boy who was easily influenced; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are repeatedly asking this question about the age of Mr. Landzo. He was five years younger than now, so that that is not a problem, to establish his age. If he could be influenced, I think he would also be influenced in a positive way, not only in a negative way. I think that he probably also feels remorse for some of the things that he has done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But you would agree that he was about 18 or 19 years old in 1992; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had -- he was five years younger than he is today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Since you were released from Celebici on July 17th 1992, you do not know when Mr. Landzo left Celebici to join the military police, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was not coming to town, so I was not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I pass the witness, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Cross-examined by MR. O'SULLIVAN

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Good morning, Professor O'Sullivan. The witness is yours now.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Eugene O'Sullivan and I represent Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I will be asking you a few questions to which I will be seeking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to say, first, that I will be seeking clarification on certain points you have already spoken about here in this Tribunal, and for that reason I will have to go over some details with you about your previous testimony; all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, I would like to ask a little bit about MUP. We have heard a lot about MUP from you. It is correct in the municipality of Konjic the police force was known as MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And MUP is the police of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war there were Serb, Croat and Muslim members of MUP; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, it is correct to say that in the municipality of Konjic MUP was very powerful and had full authority in the municipality at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As in all other municipalitites it was the same case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk a little bit about your arrest. In June 1992 you said you were arrested by the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not arrested. I surrendered to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who took you in you knew personally; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few questions about them. The leader of that group, Darko Verkic, is a Croat, is he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Aga Jozic is Croatian, is he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jozic. Pardon me. He is a Croat as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mario Maric is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my neighbour, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you also mentioned a man named Vranic, who is also a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vranic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well was not Miro Brekalo there when you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brekalo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me: at that time the HVO military police and MUP worked closely together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were not working closely together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It is also your knowledge that MUP had its own command structure with people like a Chief of Police and a Police Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few questions about the time that Mladen Zovko questioned you at Celebici. Mladen Zovko is a Croat, is he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he is a police officer, but is it not also true that he had a law degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that during your interview with him he behaved correctly and wrote down what you told him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For clarification again, he put you in the first category of prisoners, the prisoners who were considered the most dangerous; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. Probably he did. I was detained in Number 9 and people were saying that we were the first ones who are going to be executed. Whether we were dangerous or not I don't know that. I don't think we were dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not asking you whether you thought you were dangerous, but he put you in the first category and prisoners in the first category were considered the most dangerous?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered. This witness has already stated, both now and in previous cross-examination, that he did not know exactly what category he was put in. He assumed certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can remind the witness of what he said in November 1996, when he met with the representative of the Prosecution's Office. At that time, in November 1996, when you had the meeting with that individual, you said: "He put me in the first category of prisoners, that is the most dangerous prisoners." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that I did say that, but here I say another group.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here anything could be written, category 5 or 10. Here my signature is not correct. The way this is signed here, it is not how I sign, so I don't know what group I was put in. I was told that I was in the first group, when they were mistreating me, and when they abused me, they were telling me that I was in the first group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps there is some confusion here. I am referring to the statement you made in November, November 11th, 1996, when you were interviewed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interpretation is not coming through. Yes, I can hear now. There was no interpretation into Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, I am not referring to that document you have in front of you. I want to take you back to November 1996, when you were interviewed by a representative of the Office for the Prosecutor. At that time you said in your statement that: "Mladen Zovko put me in the first category of prisoners, that is the most dangerous prisoners." I am asking you to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that I did say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that Mladen Zovko was a member of the military investigation committee at Celebici, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that. I was questioned by him and what he was, where he belonged, that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you knew there was a military investigation committee at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At what time are you saying that I knew that? We were questioned by people. I assumed that there was a committee, since they had a right to question us, but I cannot answer that question, who he was, what his function was. I can't speak to that. I know that he was correct towards me. I saw him then, and then never before.
