utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let him follow your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please, I suppose you heard the objection from the defence and you heard also the comment by the Presiding Judge, so it is important to give answers to my answers (sic). I can understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I cannot just say simply "yes" and "no". I am not in Celebici. I am not in the silo. I am not in Musala. I am not in Trnovo. Please allow me to respond completely in details. If necessary, we can stay here for one year so that in details we spell everything out from A to Z. I recognise this court and I want to tell what I have lived through.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have now seen a perfect example of what my objection was about. This witness has come here with certain things in mind to tell the court. I suggest very strongly that the court admonish this witness that he will be removed as a witness if he cannot listen to the questions and answer the questions; otherwise he has no business being here. This is a court of law, not a place to make speeches. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we will get to the root of it. We will get him to answer questions which are related to what he is here to testify for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, with great respect, the witness cannot be allowed to defy the control of the court in the way he has just done so. That is intolerable and it is not the way it should be done. In my submission to your Honour, he must be told in the clearest terms that he cannot do as he wishes. It must be in answer to the questions which he is asked and under the control of learned counsel for the prosecution. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Occasionally you meet witnesses of this nature, but I think we will make him to answer questions directed to him in the way counsel wants him to answer. I do not think he will behave differently. He will try and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is always a problem for a counsel leading through a witness like Mr. Kuljanin, who has so much on his mind, and understandably so, but I see the point. It is also troublesome to interrupt the witness as soon as he has started to answer a question, but I will do my best to keep on asking the questions in as proper a way as possible. I will proceed now with introducing a document and have it marked for identification and shown to the -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: There are three difficulties. Do you know where actually you have stopped with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I know we stopped when he had entered -- yes, I know, your Honour, indeed -- when he had entered into Hangar 6 and from there I will bring him further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think you had asked him how many persons were there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You had asked him how many persons were there at the time. He had already answered that question earlier. He said about 20. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So we now know where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We move into Hangar Number 6. To do that I want to introduce this document, with the usher's assistance, please. This is a sketch attached to his statement and it will be given to the defence lawyers now. It is already in your possession. There are two documents. One is a translation of things written on the document. Now I ask you, Mr. Kuljanin: do you recognise this sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who made it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I did it myself, in my own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court what is on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This sketch is a sketch of Hangar Number 6 and how people were arranged there, and also where the dead people were after they were killed, where they were thrown in, and then they died there: Cedo Avramovic, Zeljko Cecez and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first question I will put to you is this one: how many -- maybe I should -- now it is authenticated, I will ask to introduce this as evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Which of them? There are two of them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: There are two of his sketches.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The same sketch, but one is translated from Serbo-Croat into English. That is the same sketch, just a translation. May I introduce this? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I will ask how many people were in the hangar when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived there were approximately 50 people. Not exactly 50, but around 50 people in the hangar, and about 20 of us, so altogether around 70 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anybody tell you where to sit or be in this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point no. No one told us where to sit down or how to sit down. The one who kicked me made me fall down and I just crawled to a place, and I didn't know who was around me and what people were doing there and why they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to probably stop doing this in a moment, but the question was: "Were you told to sit in a particular place?" JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: And the answer was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer was really simply "no", but we got another speech about the one who kicked him did this and the one who did that did that. If the witness could simply answer the question, we could be through here much quicker. This is going to take a long time if he is has to make a speech every time. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Frankly, counsel, you cannot do without one or two witnesses sometimes behaving in that particular way. You have to tolerate some of them. I agree we will try to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, it saved me the next question, which was: where did you land? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we will have a short break for thirty minutes and then come back and continue. (4.00 pm) (Short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. Mr. Karabdic has been delayed for a couple of minutes trying to get some paperwork done. I just wanted to inform the court that he will be in in a second. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: All right. We will accommodate you. (Witness returned to court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr. Ostberg, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The question I was going to put to you before the break was: where did you sit or place yourself in this location? It is now on the ELMO, so if you can use the pointer and point in this hangar where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not understand the interpretation. I don't know what language this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Try to find the language you can understand. Maybe you can have help from the usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My question was: where did you sit in this hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar I sat at this place that is marked here. The entrance was here and I sat here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you remain in the same place during your stay in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the general conditions? First of all, how long did you stay in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the hangar 96 days. After that I was transferred to the sports hall in Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You are referring to Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Hangar 6 are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask you to tell us about the general conditions. Start with -- what about food? How was the food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was hardly any food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There must have been some? What did you get. Try to tell us what you get a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the best of cases we would get sometimes two pieces of bread, which were so thin that you could almost see through them. In addition we would get some kind of soup, but not every day. Sometimes three days would go by without us getting anything. Then they would give us something, and then again nothing for a day or so. Then on one occasion they brought us some kind of liver paste, which we shared amongst four of us. Another time when they brought this liver paste eight of us had to share it. In any event there was not enough food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if this was the case during all the 96 days, or if it differed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the end it changed a little, because they allowed women who were somewhere nearby, mostly women living in Cerici, Celebici or Donje Selo could bring some food to the gate and hand it in at the gate. However, what happened was that often, not always, but often they would take that food and throw it into the stream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is "they"? "They would take the food". Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "They" are guards. The people who were near the gates, the guards, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the drinking supply then? Did you have any water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would get water occasionally. There was too much water actually, because when it was cold, Zenga would pour water on us, and we had to lie down on the concrete, and when it was hot --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga is from this side the second with earphones on his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That was not exactly what I asked you. I asked you who he was. I would like you to say his real name. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know his real name, nor did I ever learn it. They called him Zenga and Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know this person by the name of Zenga and Landzo and that is all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know his real name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he one of the guards who guarded you there in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he one of the guards for the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. It has been answered again. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many guards were guarding the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. They changed often. Some of them were there for longer periods of time; others for shorter. In any event, he was there for some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can give you the names that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. I am just finishing with the general conditions. Can you say something about the toilet facilities, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I showed you that there was a hole, a pit that was dug, and that is where we went for toilet needs, but often they would not let us go out, so apologies for having to say this in court, but people would do it in their pants, and then they would be beaten for it and said: "What kind of a man are you, you Chetnik?" They again would not allow people to go to urinate. We would be taken out in groups, 10, 15, 20. It differed. When we got there, the first person who got there, he could do his job, but the last man, he would start or not start and then he would wet his pants, or they would fire and interrupt him. So it was terrible. It was unbearable, you see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me also say in connection with the toilet --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are just looking for an objection now when you start telling us but I think we would finish, if possible, with the -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let us hear what the objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Prosecutor was proceeding now to ask another question. The witness was going off answering something else. He said he then wanted to make a statement and he was proceeding to make a statement that may or may not have been related to the question, but the Prosecutor said he immediately had another question, so I do not have an objection at this point. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I was about to ask you about if there was some medical care given to you in case of need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some Serb prisoners, but they could not decide about anything, nor did they have any medicines. About ten times I looked for help and the doctor would come and see me and he would just shrug his shoulders and say: "There's nothing I can do." He would say this very quietly. He would whisper this to me. "It's not up to me", he would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any kind of mistreatment of the detainees in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was plenty of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Start, Mr. Kuljanin, and tell us what happened to you personally by the way of mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a lot of those occasions so I don't know where to start from. I don't know whether I am even remembering everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you should easily -- the easiest way is to do it chronologically. When were you first beaten in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the hangar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar I was beaten several times. On one of those occasions I was taken out by guard Salko. He asked for money from me and gold. That was just behind the Hangar Number 6 (pointing). He took me out here and he beat me here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness is now pointing on the -- seen from the side of the court on the left short side of the hangar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took me out here and he beat me here (pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me in what way he did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took me out behind the hangar. I turned towards the hangar, had to raise my arms like this, (demonstrating) and he hit me with his leg. He kicked me several times here in the ribs. I fell. Then he kicked me again and with his rifle butt he hit me. He beat me for about ten or fifteen minutes, as I had no money or gold. They had already taken that from me. Then he told me to run to the hangar. As far as I could, I went slowly. I couldn't run. At that point Zenga appeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness is now pointing on the other side of the hangar, the other short side. Yes. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing). I was heading towards the entrance. Zenga appeared and he asked Salko what had happened. Salko said: "One of ours was killed and that's why I'm beating him." I didn't expect Zenga to hit me, but he hit me five or six times with his butt in the chest and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His "butt" is the butt of what, a butt of -- he hit you "with a butt" and that is the butt of -- did you lose the sound? Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He hit you with a butt and I wondered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of his rifle. It is called the Papovka rifle, a semi-automatic rifle. There was a knife at the end of it. Anyway, he hit me five or six times and then I entered the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first beating you were submitted to -- subjected to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure. I am not sure I can remember chronologically, but I will tell you everything that happened. Then television station reporters came. I think they must be the local TV reporters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not catch what you said. Who came? Who came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A man with a camera. I think he must have been from the local Konjic TV station. Zenga took me out, together with Spaso Miljevic, Velimir Dordic and Risto Vukalo. He made me sit here next to the entrance. He said to Risto Vukalo: "You will say that you were in Mostar, that you had killed people, that you had slaughtered, that you had raped people." To me he said that I had to say that I was a Chetnik from Serbia, that I had butchered people, that I had raped. To Velimir Dordic he said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "He" in this account, who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga, Zenga, Zenga. I said Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As he was working in the military garrison, he was an electrician, I think by occupation, he had to say that he had armed the Serbs, that he had given them ammunition, and I don't know what else. To Spaso Miljevic again he said that he should say something, in any event, that he had killed, that he had -- did that sort of thing. As Risto Vukalo refused to say that, he took him out of the hangar somewhere. He forced him to take off his clothes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that something you saw or is this something -- did you see somebody being taken out? Did you see somebody being taken out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him take out Risto Vukalo somewhere. I did not see how he beat him or what he beat him with, but when he came back he was all blue. Then Risto Vukalo told me later that he had taken a belt and hit him so hard with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object to what Risto Vukalo told him because we cannot possibly cross-examine Risto Vukalo. It violates the rules of confrontation, the right of confrontation. Unless Mr. Vukalo is here as a witness, we cannot possibly challenge what Mr. Vukalo says. Therefore we object to what he says Mr. Vukalo said. I have no objection to him talking about what he saw and what he heard himself but not from a witness who cannot be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: To me this is not a valid -- a moment, Mr. Kuljanin,. Let us settle this first. To me this is not a valid objection. This belongs to what he saw. He saw a man being taken out. A man came back and told what happened to him. That belongs to his testimony. To me this is something the court should hear. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Objection: it is what he said Vukalo told him. That is a different thing from what he said he observed of Vukalo when he came back. They are two different things. So what he said he told him would not be evidence in this respect. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the court what you saw on this person who came back. What did he look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he entered he was all black and blue, all over the body entirely and he went to his place and sat down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come back by himself or did somebody bring him back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came by himself, because he wasn't really beaten up but he hit him with a belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So you could see the bruises all over from his forehead to his heels. They were not very strong beatings, but this is with a belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So he came by himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you proceed to tell us about the next mistreatment you were subjected to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that Zenga put a bomb in my mouth and told me that I had to say what he had told me to say, that I had killed. I couldn't say that because I hadn't done it. Then he wanted to kick me by turning around at the chest, but my reflexes reacted so I somehow protected myself. He did it twice, and after that he told me: "Go back to your place. I'll come back at 1 am and you'll see what lies in wait for you." He used a swearword. I apologise. He didn't come that night. Then later when the people from Sandzak came, he took off my shoes and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "He" again; are you still talking about Zenga? Be careful to tell exactly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on with your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am talking about Zenga. I was saying that when the Sandzak people came Zenga was with them and Delic was with them too and they came along this side and Delic with these people from Sandzak and Zenga came along this side. He reached me. He took my shoes off and with his boots he stepped on his heel pressing down hard asking me: "How are you?" What could I do but say: "I am all right." Then he passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For clarification you named: "He came with ..." and then the names, some people. What kind of people were that? You said: "Zenga came with ..." and then you had a name for the group of people. I did not quite get what kind of people that was. Were they soldiers or civilians? What were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers. They were soldiers from the region known as Sandzak. I know very well the accent all over Yugoslavia, because I travelled a lot before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were they -- from what kind of army were these soldiers? What kind of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were -- they belonged to the Muslim army. They were the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they serve as guards or as something else in the Celebici detention centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not guards in the Celebici camp. They came as visitors. They came round to see us and beat us up. Of course I saw that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was one incident, what happened when these soldiers were there. Can you then proceed if you have further types of mistreatment to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I personally am concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic would come and he would give us all slaps. He would slap us all. On one occasion Zenga forced me with a stick, a baseball stick like this, to make -- to use the -- to do ten push-ups. Then he would hit me. Another time he did not have the bat, but he kicked me, usually on the right-hand side, while I was doing -- while we were doing push-ups. Then he would say "up to ten", and then he would let us go, but usually he would start beating at 3, 4, 5. Then he would let us go on until number 8 and then he would hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Kuljanin,. Did this take place in the hangar or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar. In the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many times things like this with the push-ups happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me personally twice, and the other people many more times. Some people only once. Some never, but there were people who were daily, and I could give you their names too, who were mistreated daily and beaten up, but it happened to me personally twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did something else happen to you like this mistreatment more than you have already told us? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He said twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, for the push-ups. Go on to other events apart from the push-ups and what you told us previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did it very frequently in front of us with Vukasin Mrkajic, Risto Vukalo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now proceeding to tell us what you saw happened to other people or are you going to tell us that something more happened to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other people. Please tell us what you saw yourself, what happened to other people and tell us at the same time who did it, please. You named somebody. Go on. Give the name again and tell us what you saw happen to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vukasin Mrkajic was sitting around here, his back to the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, so we can see on the ELMO where you point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I cannot find it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here. (Indicating). He had his back to the door and I was sitting here so that I could see, you see. Zenga every day -- I don't know what torture he did not employ on him. Every day he had to do push-ups. I don't know what he didn't do. He beat him over the back and legs with a rifle butt. I am telling everything that was going on in the hangar. The same with Risto Vukalo. The same tortures were subjected to him. Then Dusko Bendjo, he was sitting around here. He was doing the same things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked me, when you name people, you name them slowly so they have a chance to put down who they really happened to. Now you mentioned a name. I could not clearly understand what the name was of this person. Bendo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Bendo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusan or Dusko. I don't know. One of those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In any event he was called Dusko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that is what happened to him every day. They beat him. They were accusing him of some things. He was a taxi driver before the war. He had money. On one occasion Zenga took him out and asked him for money and -- let me point. (Pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are pointing on the side of -- I could not see where you did point really. I could not see where you pointed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front here where I was sitting. I was sitting in the hangar here and I could hear what he was asking him. He was asking him for money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he", is that Zenga you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear through the wall of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't a wall really. It was a tin plate. It wasn't very thick. There was a crack underneath. Somewhere it was 1 cm, somewhere it was more underneath. So he didn't have money and then he beat him. He was weeping and he was saying: "There's a car in front of my house. I don't have any money. Take the car." That went on for about half an hour. He brought him back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And "he" again is Zenga in this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zenga. I am talking about Zenga now. Then later the others will come up. Then Zenga did that to Radoslav Kuljanin who sat here close to me. Zenga did that to Zoran Djordjic, who was sitting close to him, and I could see it. Next --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say what he did to them? I could not see that on the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly he beat them with a stick. It is like a baseball bat. He kicked them with his boots, then forced them to do push-ups and would kick them while they were doing it. On one occasion he took out two brothers and he forced them to perform a certain act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please if you just take a little pause, I will ask the court that we go into private session for the upcoming three or four questions on the same grounds that we have done that before. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Instruct them to do it. The technicians can do it. (In private session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You mentioned many names of people who you saw being mistreated in the hangar. Have you exhausted your list or did you see more things that you have yet not told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is enough stuff for five days' worth of talking. See this sketch here, there is Scepo Gotovac here who was taken out. Then there is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I am going to do now, I would ask you to separate these beatings from what we now, I suppose, are going to discuss, if you saw any killings. Have we exhausted the list of what you will tell us about beatings in the hangar? Thank you. Then, your Honour, I want to -- just a moment, Mr. Kuljanin -- I want to introduce a document, again in two pieces, in Serbo-Croat and in translation into English. I will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Can we have them marked for identification? This document is also attached to the statement so it is already in the possession of the defence, but they will also have a copy now if they need it. Just a moment. I will give you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was just not finished with --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document which is now shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you -- did you also write the text on the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the numbers and the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The numbers -- there is a seal, but the numbers preceding the names I wrote them down myself and the list of names I also wrote them down myself, except I was not quite finished with the tortures yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us do this first before we enter this list then. Do you have something to add about the tortures? Please do it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this short period of time one cannot recall everything. Let me bring this back. Here in this place around Spaso Miljevic was sitting and he was tortured quite often. Often he was called out and taken out and beaten. On one occasion he came back. He had been burned. You could see. They were putting something under his fingernails. I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Kuljanin, can you tell us who took him out? Who took him out? You said "they" took him out. We really want to know who did it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly it was the guards who did it. Sometimes -- and I will say that later -- but in 90 per cent of the cases Zenga was the one who was calling them out. He had a very characteristic, very specific voice. You could not not recognise him, whether it was in the dead of night or in broad daylight. In other words, he would call people out and take them out with a group of his. I don't know how many there were, or whether he was alone there. I cannot say what went on outside, but in 90 per cent of the cases he was the one who called people out and he would take people out, and every night --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought them back, these people who were taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people were able to return on their own and some were carried in, usually by the people who were sitting next to the door, and they would say: "Come on. We need two to come out and bring him in." That was not just once. It was very often, at night, and usually it was the people sitting next to the door. They had to -- sometimes they would bring the person in. Not always, but sometimes it would happen that a person could come in on his own power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Kuljanin, in this context is: did this go on during all the time you stayed in the hangar, or was it on specific times, and I would also be very happy if you could give the approximate time when different things happened by naming the month or date, if you can. It is interesting to know. You told us you were sitting there 96 days. My question would be: did this happen all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the International Red Cross visit, which was on 12th August, 12th August it diminished. In fact, it let up quite a bit, but until that visit of the Red Cross the tortures were happening daily. Now whether it was from a single guard, whether from different guards or groups. For instance, they would come from Konjic, people who were not guards there. For instance, Maca, somebody whose nickname was Maca, he came there frequently and he beat people, threatened them. Then in the beginning there was a guard named Kravar, and then he was transferred, but he would come in occasionally. Then the groups that would come in at night, they would call people out and beat them, mistreated them. If they had had an argument and a quarrel ten or fifteen years previously, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Non-responsive. This is the same speech-making that we have had before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can we confine the answers to exactly what you saw and not talk about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Tell us what happened in that place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You saw all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that. I saw Maca when he came and Miljanic. I can't recall his first name. He sat about here. Why and how no one knows. Kravar, Kravar took me out once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is still non-responsive. The question was: "Did this happen every day?" or "Did it happen all the time?" That requires a "yes", "no" or "maybe", or couple of sentences to explain it. We have had about five minutes now on: "Did this happen every day?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 96 days there were maybe five or six days when it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think you have exhausted your very long list of torture and mistreatment in the hangar? There could be still more to tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have another example, try to make them short and name the people which it happened to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In short and to make it short and clear, Nedeljko Samoukovic sat here, who was my friend from school. He was accused of some things. Delic did it as well as Zenga. They would come and beat him with sticks. Next, Momir Kuljanin sat here, close to me, one place away from me. Zenga called him out one night. Then he came back and his hand was like this from the blister, both big and swollen (indicating). Next, Jovo Draganic from Brdjani, he was also called out. He was beaten. There was a group of guards. I think he was called out by Hasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the word "I think." You are not sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovo Draganic, he was called out one night and was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. It is still non-responsive. The question was: "Are you sure?" That response bears no relationship to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The question is: did you see Hasim Delic do anything to this person? Did you? Did you see Hazim Delic do anything to this person you named?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him do it, but the man was carried in and he lay down there immobile for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Non-responsive. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No, he has said he did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That was -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is exclusionary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That was fine. It is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you still have examples? I am certain you could go on, but on the other hand we have been given so many. We know how awful it all was. If you have some more, in your mind very illustrative examples, I should ask you to give them and then we will close this list of people tortured. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: If they are relevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zjelko Klimenta was also called out and after he came back he lay there for two days and nights. He was beaten up. I am talking about the guards who were there. They returned him and he was beaten up and two or three days later they took him to the infirmary and he was there for about 20 days. He came back and I saw his forearms. They were both crooked. He said: "As long as I am alive, I can fix that," going to surgery, I guess. Then Radoslav Kuljanin was called out, again by a group of guards. He was beaten up and he lay here for two or three days, but motionless. He could not move. He could not budge. Nobody could help him. We had no food or water to give him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just gave you the list and you have authenticated it, and I will ask your Honours to admit that into evidence. I will ask Mr. Kuljanin, about these people on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will object to its admission into evidence. It is, of course, an out of court document. It is not a document that was prepared here in this court room. The question is whether the information contained on it comes from personal knowledge or comes from things this witness might have heard. There has been no foundation to establish that what this witness placed on that list came from his own personal knowledge, and my concern, therefore, is about the reliability of the names that are put on that list and where this witness came by the supposed knowledge that caused him to create this list. So I think until there has been a further foundation with regard to whether or not this witness has personal knowledge of the information contained on this document, that it should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I accept that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what I thought Mr. Ostberg was going to do. He is going to refer to all these killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will try to substantiate just that one by one to see if this list is made out of personal knowledge. I am starting from the beginning and ask you about Petko Gligorevic. Can you briefly tell us what you saw happen to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I prepared this list and this was according to my memory as to how many people were killed. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The question is: what do you know happened to Petko Gligorevic? That is the question. Try and tell the Trial Chamber what you know happened to him. He is taking you through one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Petko Gligorevic was brought to the camp, he was killed right at the beginning. He succumbed to the beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see that. His son saw it and he was with me and I know that he was killed in the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes it about Petko Gligorevic. What about Gojo Miljanic? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He said he did not see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gojo Miljanic was also killed while he was being brought and again his son was present and he was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am going to object. The appropriate question was whether he has any personal knowledge or not. He is just giving, you know -- who knows where this came from? The Prosecutor said: "We will prove this up by starting with Petko" and the first answer we get is he has no idea except what he heard from somebody. So I think the foundation is not laid unless the Prosecutor asks the witness: "Do you have personal knowledge? Did you see? Did you observe? Do you know of your own personal knowledge?" That is what is not being done. All of this is coming in through totally unreliable hearsay, I think. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You are getting overly anxious. We are trying to show if he has not any personal knowledge of the list which he had indicated, then it will not be evidence for the purpose of the list he has given. That is what we are trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The first thing -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is not enough merely to produce a list like this example. It must be a list based on his actual knowledge of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: As the learned counsel may have heard, I started by saying what he knew from personal knowledge and that was my first question. Then the next one: was what do you know about number one? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is a little bit two-way. It could be information he got somehow. If he did not see these things, it might not be correct to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Right. Gojo Miljanic, did you see anything concerning Gojo Miljanic personally. Answer my question first: did you see anything personally about this man, Gojo Miljanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think we will leave him and go to number 3? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, that is what you should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Because if you look at the heading, what he indicated is this is a list of killings. He must be able to justify these things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the list from my memory of the people who were killed in the camp. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We have omitted the first three now. It is not your personal knowledge;. You did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Now we can to Zjelko Klimenta, number four. Did you see personally what happened to Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zjelko Klimenta --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is easier if you start with if you saw anything personally concerning him instead of telling us first. Tell us first if you saw it or did not see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see concerning Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relating to Klimenta, the day before his death at 5 or 6 o'clock Kovacic came and brought him a pack of cigarettes. Hazim Delic came into the hangar and I personally heard what he was talking to Klimenta. He brought him this pack of cigarettes and he said: "Zjelko, here is cigarettes. Have you heard of Ibe?" He said: "Yes, I have." At that point behind Hasim Delic said: "Why are you giving him the cigarettes? Fuck him. He is not going to be alive tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you heard personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, personally. I heard the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Then what happened to Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he was giving him the cigarettes this one said that from behind. This was in the evening of 26th July, 27th July in the morning. I don't know the exact time, 4 or 5 in the morning they called out Zjelko Klimenta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who called him out? Do you remember who called him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall, but in any event it was the guards. They called him out together with Predrag Kujundzic and another one, a third person, but I can't recall who that was. I can't recall the third person. They took him out and about ten minutes later a bullet was heard firing and the other two ran back in with their heads -- with their hands holding their heads. Predrag Kujundzic was in tears and we know right away what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection again. Non-responsive. The question was: "Do you remember who called him out?" We are getting a speech and not an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I think we got some names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards. It was the guards. I don't know who the guards were at that time but it was the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No name. You saw him go out after having been called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He already said it so I do not have to ask it again. Do you have anything more to add concerning Klimenta of your own, things you have seen yourself. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He did not see anything. He saw them call him out and then later he heard a shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. We go to the next one. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we will have to stop here. We will continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: adjourned at 5.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of May, 1997 at 10 a.m. 24 25
